title: Etalon: Holistic Performance Evaluation Framework for LLM Inference Systems
technique: METRIC-PAPER: proposes deadline-based fluidity-index and fluid token generation rate (with capacity search) to replace TTFT/TBT/TPOT/normalized-latency for user-facing evaluation

optimized_metrics.evidence: fluidity-index accounts this variability by setting token-level deadlines and measuring the fraction of deadlines met within a request.
fluid token generation rate complements fluidity-index by determining the maximum sustainable playback rate that maintains a specified level of fluidity (e.g., fluidity-index > 0.9).
it becomes possible to report the maximum load the system can sustain (capacity), subject to SLOs defined on fluidity-index, e.g., 99% of requests achieving a metric of ≥ 0.9.

headline_claim.text: we first identify the pitfalls of current performance metrics in evaluating LLM inference systems. We then propose Etalon, a comprehensive performance evaluation framework that includes fluidity-index– a novel metric designed to reflect the intricacies of the LLM inference process and its impact on real-time user experience.

metric_definitions.definition_quote: Time To First Token (TTFT) [32, 7] is the latency between the request arrival and the first output token generated by the system for the request. It includes the scheduling delay (time elapsed from request arrival to start of prompt processing) and the prompt processing time.
Time Between Tokens (TBT) [17] is the latency of every subsequent token generation in the decode phase. This metric directly influences the perceived speed of the model by users.

Time Per Output Token (TPOT) [32, 7] is closely related to TBT. It is the average time to generate an output token in the decode phase. It is calculated as the total decode time of a request normalized by the number of decode tokens generated.

This is defined as the total execution time of a request normalized by the number of decode tokens. It includes the scheduling delay, prompt processing time and time to generate all the decode tokens. Median Normalised Latency has been used in [30, 25] to compare system throughput.
This is defined as the maximum request load (queries-per-second) a system can sustain while meeting certain latency targets (SLOs).

Let the desired TTFT and TBT for a given application be Dp and Dd, respectively. Note that Dp will be a function of the number of prefill tokens. We then define the deadline for the generation of the ith token as Di = Dp + i × Dd.

We then define a deadline-miss as an event when the actual token generation time of the ith token exceeds Di. ... if there was a deadline-miss at the sth token, we reset the deadlines for all subsequent tokens to be Di = ts + (i − s) × Dd, where ts is the actual generation time of the sth token
metric_definitions.notes: slack from early tokens is carried forward as a buffer; a stall counts as floor((t-slack-D)/Dd)+1 misses (Algorithm 1)
per-request fraction of token deadlines met; prefill deadline D_p = predict_prefill_time(P) + SD (scheduling slack); 'deadline-based TBT acceptance rate metric'

metric_definitions.definition_quote: we find the minimum TBT SLO Dd such that 99% percent of the requests have fluidity-index of at-least 0.9. The inverse of this is the fluid token generation rate.
metric_definitions.notes: tokens/s; black-box; inverse of the min TBT deadline meeting the fluidity SLO

metric_definitions.definition_quote: we plot the inverse of the observed mean TPOT across all requests, and the inverse of the 99th percentile TBT.

We use fluidity-index to define the service SLO as – 99% of requests should have less than 10% deadline miss rate with 25ms target TBT. Etalon then finds the maximum request load (QPS) at which the SLOs can be maintained.

metric_critiques.critique_quote: TTFT, which measures prefill efficiency, includes both the scheduling delay ... and the actual prompt processing time which depends on the prompt length. Naively comparing two systems on their TTFT does not reveal the individual contribution of these components to the prefill time. Moreover, since TTFT is highly dependent on the prompt length (quadratic) ... defining a static Service Level Objective (SLO) on TTFT ... is not practical.

Normalized latency hides scheduling delay. ... the scheduling delay is above 25s for almost 60% of the requests in vLLM, compared to Sarathi-Serve which has a maximum scheduling delay of 15s. However, the normalized latency for these systems differs only be a few hundred milliseconds!

Time Per Output Token (TPOT) and normalised latency hides jitters in token generation. ... vLLM suffers a long stall of 10s ... the impact of this stall on the TPOT or normalized latency metric will be numerically small due to the normalization by (typically) large number of decode tokens.
tail latency does not reveal the complete profile of magnitude and frequency of stalls at request level

TBT CDFs do not reveal the magnitude and temporal characteristics of stalls. ... a high tail TBT could have potentially occurred at the start of token generation, disrupting the user experience at the start itself. This is not captured by the TBT CDF.
TBT fails to account for non-uniform token generation strategies. Techniques such as speculative decoding can generate multiple decode tokens for the same request in a single iteration.

a system which produces 10 tokens at TBT of 10ms and the 11th token at TBT of 150ms, will see the same TBT miss rate as a system which produces 10 tokens at TBT of 100ms and the 11th token at TBT of 150ms. Clearly the first system is much more superior than the second, but the TBT miss rate itself does not capture that.

while TPOT downplays the discrepancies between the systems, tail-TBT overstates them. Neither metric accurately reflects the true system throughput under constraints of quality of service or user experience.

Groq has the highest throughput of 600 tokens/s based on TPOT, a value that service providers oftentimes report. However, the tail TBT metric shows a 4× lesser throughput ... The former is too relaxed and ignores generation stalls while the latter over penalizes the tail latency spikes.

recommended_practice.quote: Etalon provides a capacity evaluation module, which evaluates a system with different request loads to identify the maximum capacity each replica can provide while meeting the fluidity-index SLO requirements.
We define three targets in Etalon– a strict target for interactive applications like chat (25ms), medium target for medium-priority users (50ms) and a relaxed target for low-priority users (100ms).

in Etalon, we propose Dp to be a function of prompt length. We use a reasonable open-source system like vLLM as baseline to benchmark the prefill time as a function of input length by profiling the request in isolation ... the process of identifying this prefill latency curve should be repeated on the system being evaluated
Since the performance of public APIs can change throughout the day depending on request traffic and other factors, we run Etalon once every hour for 24 hours

slo_spec: Fluidity SLO: 99% of requests achieve fluidity-index >= 0.9 (deadline miss <10%); decode TBT target Dd 25/50/100 ms (strict/medium/relaxed); prefill target Dp a function of prompt length fitted from isolated profiling on vLLM (10 requests) plus scheduling slack
load_regime: request-rate sweep (capacity search); black-box hourly runs over 24h for public APIs
tradeoff_acknowledged: Under a 25ms P99-TBT SLO Sarathi-Serve capacity is 2x lower than vLLM, whereas under fluidity-index both are the same at 0.6 QPS (metric choice flips the ranking); tail TBT gives vLLM 3x worse throughput than Sarathi while TPOT shows parity
hardware: H100 (vLLM/Sarathi-Serve, Llama3-8B); 2xH100 (Yi-34B motivation); public APIs for Anyscale, Groq, Fireworks
workloads: Arxiv-Summarization, ShareGPT, LMSys-Chat-1M (stats), custom 256-8k prompt workload
